scope: Named foreign shareholders (≥1%) of NIFTY 50 constituents, from primary SEBI Reg. 31(1)(b) shareholding-pattern filings opened directly on five companies' own investor-relations sites (Reliance Industries, HDFC Bank, ITC, Bharti Airtel, State Bank of India — chosen for sector and ownership-structure spread: diversified conglomerate, private bank, FMCG with a legacy colonial FDI stake, telecom with a foreign strategic promoter, and a majority-government PSU bank), plus FII/FPI aggregate percentages (screener.in, an aggregator, cross-checked against the five primary filings' own totals) for ten further constituents. This is a documented sample of 15 of the 50 NIFTY 50 constituents, not the full index: the fetch budget (25–40) does not stretch to 50 individual SEBI filings at 1–3 fetches each, so this file goes deep on five and wide-but-shallow on ten more, and says so rather than padding with unopened aggregator summaries presented as named-holder data. It covers: the mandatory comparison set (BlackRock, Vanguard, Norges Bank Investment Management/Government Pension Fund Global, GIC/Government of Singapore, Capital Group, Fidelity, Kuwait Investment Authority, ADIA) tested against every company actually opened; LIC as the domestic control; two foreign holders found in the data that are outside the comparison set but material (GQG Partners in ITC, Google International LLC in Bharti Airtel); the two foreign strategic/promoter stakes that dwarf any passive FPI line (British American Tobacco in ITC via three wholly-owned vehicles, Suzuki Motor Corporation in Maruti Suzuki) and Singtel's promoter-group vehicle in Bharti Airtel; and the JioBlackRock asset-management/advisory joint venture. It leaves out, by design: adviser mandates (Rothschild & Co vs Lazard/Goldman Sachs/Morgan Stanley/JPMorgan/Citi/Kotak/Axis Capital/Avendus) — a distinct question for a companion file this pass did not produce; the World Bank/IMF/multilateral-loan narrative, which belongs to the finance fleet; and the Soros/OSF funding narrative, which belongs to the ngo fleet. NBIM's own nbim.no holdings-search tool was probed and found to be a client-side JS application whose backing API could not be located through the proxy (static HTML shell only, ~27KB on every route tried); NBIM's per-company India percentages here therefore come from the Indian companies' own disclosures, which name Norges Bank's fund as 'Government Pension Fund Global', not from NBIM's own site — recorded as a void below, not silently worked around.

d: Not found as a named ≥1% shareholder in any of the five NIFTY 50 companies whose SEBI shareholding-pattern filings were opened directly in this pass (Reliance Industries, HDFC Bank, ITC, Bharti Airtel, State Bank of India), each as of its most recent quarter (Jun 2026 / Jun 2026 / Dec 2025 / Dec 2025 / Mar 2025) [documented, absence in a 5-of-50 sample]

This is consistent with how BlackRock invests in India: through many separately SEBI-registered FPI entities (multiple iShares ETF share classes, multiple BlackRock Global Funds sub-funds, separate institutional mandates) rather than one consolidated registration, so no single line typically crosses the 1%-of-company naming threshold even where BlackRock's combined exposure is larger — a structural reason the passive-index share of 'BlackRock owns India' is easy to overstate from any one filing [analytic inference from the filings themselves, not a documented aggregate]

JioBlackRock Asset Management Pvt Ltd and JioBlackRock Investment Advisers Pvt Ltd: 50:50 joint ventures with Jio Financial Services Ltd, each partner subscribing 5.85 crore ₹10 equity shares (₹58.5 crore each, ₹117 crore aggregate paid-in capital for the AMC); SEBI granted the AMC's mutual-fund registration 26 May 2025 and the advisory arm's registration 10 June 2025; partnership announced July 2023 [documented]

Eight US-listed iShares ETFs together hold between 0.48% (SBI) and 1.78% (Infosys) of each of the ten largest NIFTY 50 companies by index weight, as of 2026-09-24 — a lower bound on the BlackRock complex [analytic, this file]

narratives.claim: FPI money is round-tripped black money.
narratives.strongestCase: Hindenburg Research's January 2023 report on the Adani group alleged specifically that opaque, thinly disclosed offshore FPI structures were used to conceal beneficial ownership and inflate free float — an allegation serious enough that SEBI responded with new binding disclosure rules seven months later (24 August 2023: full look-through beneficial-ownership disclosure for FPIs with over 50% of India-equity AUM in one group, or over ₹25,000 crore in India equities).
narratives.strongestCounter: The named holders this file actually found ≥1% in five major NIFTY 50 constituents are, without exception, transparent-by-construction: two sovereign entities that publish their own holdings (Norway's Government Pension Fund Global, Singapore's GIC), two large regulated Western index-fund families (Vanguard, and GQG Partners which is itself SEC-registered), a strategic corporate investor with a public commercial partnership (Google), and a 130-year-old listed multinational's FDI stake (British American Tobacco in ITC). None of that is consistent with 'round-tripped black money'; the concern SEBI's 2023 rule targets is specifically the opposite pattern — funds that do not disclose, which by definition would not show up as a named ≥1% line in a company's own filing, so this file's method (reading named-holder tables) cannot itself confirm or rule out round-tripping in the undisclosed tail of FPI ownership.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: SEBI enforcement data on how many FPIs were actually forced into full look-through disclosure under the 2023 rule, and what (if anything) it revealed about beneficial ownership — not checked in this pass.
srcs: TaxGuru — 'SEBI Tightens FPI Disclosure Norms after Adani-Hindenburg'

symmetryCheck: The same five-company, primary-filing lens applied to every name in SPEC's mandatory comparison set (BlackRock, Vanguard, NBIM, GIC/Government of Singapore, Capital Group, Fidelity, Kuwait Investment Authority, ADIA) plus LIC as the domestic control produces a graded, not uniform, picture: BlackRock — the name that carries the most alarming popular narrative — crosses the 1% named-holder threshold zero times in five checks; Vanguard once; NBIM and GIC/Singapore twice each; Capital Group, Fidelity, KIA and ADIA zero times each (absence-in-small-sample, not confirmed absence). LIC, the domestic control, crosses 1% in four of five and is the single largest non-promoter shareholder in three of them. The two foreign holdings that actually dwarf every passive-fund line in the sample — British American Tobacco's 22.91% of ITC and (tier reported) Suzuki Motor Corporation's ~58% of Maruti Suzuki — are neither BlackRock nor Vanguard nor any other passive index manager: they are foreign industrial promoters, a structurally different kind of foreign ownership the 'asset managers own India' narrative does not usually mean and does not distinguish. Running the same lens on the controls therefore does not produce an equally alarming picture for BlackRock specifically — if anything the opposite, a systematic UNDER-representation relative to its reputation, for the structural reason recorded on the cap:blackrock entity (fragmentation across many separately registered FPI vehicles, none individually crossing 1%) — while it produces a genuinely large, well-documented, non-alarmist finding (a legacy multinational tobacco company's ~23% stake in India's largest FMCG conglomerate; a Japanese automaker's ~59% stake in India's largest carmaker) that the popular narrative rarely names at all.

gaps: 45 of 50 NIFTY 50 constituents were not individually checked for named ≥1% foreign holders in this pass (fetch budget); the 15 that were checked (5 with named-holder detail, 10 aggregate FII/FPI % only) are not a random sample — they skew toward the largest, most index-weighted names, which may understate fragmentation (large caps likely have more, not fewer, distinct FPI registrations, each individually smaller) relative to mid-weight NIFTY 50 names.

SEC EDGAR full-text search (efts.sec.gov, confirmed reachable in SPEC's reconnaissance) for BlackRock's and Vanguard's 13F filings on Indian ADRs (Infosys INFY, ICICI Bank IBN, HDFC Bank HDB, Wipro WIT, Dr. Reddy's RDY) was not attempted in this pass — this would show US-side beneficial ownership of Indian ADRs, a genuinely different and possibly larger-looking BlackRock/Vanguard exposure than the NSE/BSE-side FPI-registration data in this file, and should be the next check before treating this file's BlackRock finding as final.

NBIM's own nbim.no holdings-search tool render as a client-side JS application through the proxy on every route tried; per-company NBIM percentages here come from the Indian companies' own filings (which name the holder 'Government Pension Fund Global'), not from NBIM's own published database — see voids.

Capital Group (EuroPacific Growth Fund / New Perspective Fund), Fidelity, Kuwait Investment Authority and Abu Dhabi Investment Authority were not found as named ≥1% holders in the 5-company sample checked — absence in a 5-of-50 sample is not evidence of absence; none of the four is asserted here to be absent from NIFTY 50 ownership generally.

Suzuki Motor Corporation's Maruti Suzuki percentage (holders:c018) rests on screener.in (an aggregator) rather than a primary BSE/company filing — marutisuzuki.com's investor-updates page rendered as an empty ~4.7KB JavaScript shell through the proxy and no direct shareholding-pattern PDF link could be located within budget; screener.in itself shows two different figures (58.65% quarterly vs 56.28% in a differently-dated 'About' snapshot) that were not reconciled.

ITC's most recent primary filing opened is for the quarter ended 31.12.2025, one quarter behind the June-2026 filings used for Reliance Industries and HDFC Bank — a guessed URL for a 30 June 2026 ITC filing (following the site's observed naming pattern) returned a connection reset / 404 and was not pursued further within budget.

State Bank of India's most recent primary filing opened is for the quarter ended 31.03.2025, over a year behind this file's asOf date — a more recent SBI filing was referenced in search results (implying a 2025-26 quarter exists) but its direct PDF URL was not located within budget.

This file does not cover foreign adviser mandates (Rothschild & Co vs Lazard/Goldman Sachs/Morgan Stanley/JPMorgan/Citi/Kotak/Axis Capital/Avendus — deal, role, date, fee), which is a distinct SPEC requirement not produced in this pass and belongs in a companion 'advisers' file.

This file does not cover the World Bank/IMF loan-conditionality narrative (belongs to the finance fleet) or the Soros/Open Society Foundations funding narrative (belongs to the ngo fleet) — both are part of SPEC's full narrative list for the capital fleet as a whole but are out of scope for a holders-only file focused on NIFTY 50 equity ownership.
